decisions.note: The highest-urgency class in this repository, and it is not signing. The anchors are the publicly verifiable encryption paths — include-internal/cbmpc/internal/protocol/pve_base.h:213 calls prv_key.ecdh(...) and checks a 32-byte output, and src/cbmpc/api/{pve_base_pke,pve_batch_ac, pve_batch_single_recipient}.cpp plus pve_internal.h:154 all guard on "missing HSM ECIES ECDH callback". PVE is how key shares are encrypted to a recipient for backup and escrow, so the ciphertexts are stored. Harvest-now-decrypt-later applies in full: a copy taken today of an encrypted share set becomes plaintext once a CRQC exists, and no later migration undoes that. Unlike a signature scheme, this can be fixed today by wrapping the share under a hybrid KEM, which makes it the first thing to do rather than the hardest — and nearer than it looks, because this repository already implements ML-KEM-768 without the PVE path using it. See the DEP-NO-PQC-LIBRARY decision below.

Correct, with a parameter worth quoting: include-internal/cbmpc/internal/crypto/base_paillier.h declares class paillier_t with static constexpr int bit_size = 2048, so the modulus is 2048 bits and Shor's algorithm faces exactly the problem it faces for RSA-2048. The evidence is real implementation rather than a name match — base_paillier.h, zk/zk_paillier.h's valid_paillier_t, and the key structures in protocol/ecdsa_2p.h and hd_keyset_ecdsa_2p.h, which each hold a crypto::paillier_t and its c_key. This is the row that a post-quantum *signature* standard does not help with: Paillier is the homomorphic encryption the two-party ECDSA protocol is built on, so replacing it is a protocol redesign, and NIST's 2024 standards (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) are single-signer schemes that do not offer a drop-in replacement.

Correct and anchored on real parameter generation, not a mention: src/cbmpc/zk/zk_pedersen.cpp constructs pedersen_commitment_params_t with primes generated via BN_generate_prime_ex (the comment names the OpenSSL function), zk_pedersen.h:13 exposes get() and check_safe_prime_subgroup, and both src/cbmpc/protocol/ecdsa_2p.cpp:28 and src/cbmpc/zk/zk_paillier.cpp:537 pull those parameters. Stated precisely, because the distinction decides how bad this is: breaking the discrete log costs a Pedersen commitment its *binding* property, not its hiding — the commitment is perfectly hiding, so no committed value is recoverable from it even with a CRQC. The exposure is forgeability inside the proofs, i.e. future protocol soundness, not retroactive disclosure.

The claim is right — cb-mpc is a threshold ECDSA library and these 13 files are its protocol surface (api/ecdsa_2p.h, api/ecdsa_mp.h, internal/protocol/ecdsa_2p.h, ecdsa_mp.h, hd_keyset_ecdsa_2p.h) — but the cited evidence is weaker than the claim and a reader should know which is which. Most anchors are namespace declarations and their closing braces (namespace coinbase::api::ecdsa_2p, coinbase::mpc::ecdsampc), so the row follows from the library's purpose rather than from the quoted line. The substantive evidence for this class is in the Paillier and Pedersen rows above, which cite implementations. Confirmed on that basis, and the detector would serve better by anchoring on the protocol functions.

Threshold EdDSA, which the library implements alongside threshold ECDSA: api/eddsa_2p.h, internal/protocol/eddsa.h (which includes schnorr_mp.h), hd_keyset_eddsa_2p.h and src/cbmpc/api/eddsa2pc.cpp, where blob_to_key validates the key blob role. Same conclusion as threshold ECDSA and the same caveat about namespace anchors; the protocol is a Schnorr-style multiparty scheme over Ed25519, so Shor breaks both the signature and the discrete-log proofs around it.

Plain (non-threshold) ECDSA on secp256k1 inside the Schnorr two-party API: src/cbmpc/api/schnorr2pc.cpp:31 and :48 validate and write blob.curve against curve_id::secp256k1 and serialise key.Q compressed. Key-blob handling for the signing keys, so the same migration item as the threshold rows; counted separately because it is the serialisation format, which is where a migration needs a version bump.

Role resolved. src/cbmpc/crypto/base_rsa.cpp implements rsa_pub_key_t with encrypt_raw (deliberately RSA_NO_PADDING, because it is a primitive for a higher-level scheme rather than a general-purpose encryption API), verify_pkcs1, and EVP_RSA_gen(bits) for generation. It is included by internal/crypto/base_pki.h and internal/crypto/base_paillier.h and exercised by tests/unit/api/test_pve.cpp, so this is the PKI layer underneath publicly verifiable encryption and the modulus arithmetic that Paillier is built on. Same quantum exposure as the Paillier row, for the same reason: Shor factors the composite modulus. Because PVE ciphertexts are stored, this inherits the harvest-now-decrypt-later urgency of the ECDH row rather than the lower urgency of a signing path.

Accurate as written — the rule is about *declared dependency manifests*, and cb-mpc declares no PQC-capable library — but it would mislead a reader on its own, so the rest belongs here. The source tree already implements ML-KEM-768 itself: include-internal/cbmpc/internal/crypto/mlkem768.h and src/cbmpc/crypto/mlkem768.cpp define mlkem768_pub_key_t and mlkem768_prv_key_t with encapsulate and decapsulate, and the inventory carries both rows as post-quantum. What it is not is wired up: the only files that include it are its own .cpp, src/cbmpc/crypto/CMakeLists.txt and tests/unit/crypto/test_mlkem768.cpp. Nothing in the PVE or PKI path reaches it. So the accurate statement is the useful one: the KEM this library needs for its harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure is already built and not yet connected to it — a wiring job rather than a research problem. Separately, and still true: no standardised post-quantum *threshold signature* exists to depend on (NIST's 2024 standards are single-signer, the multi-party threshold effort is at the call stage, and the literature notes PQC-round schemes do not convert directly to threshold form through MPC), so the signing side of this library is the part that cannot be closed today.

findings.title: Quantum-vulnerable ECDH: key wrapping and data encryption at rest (5 file(s))
findings.description: 5 reference(s) to ECDH across 5 file(s), e.g. include-internal/cbmpc/internal/protocol/pve_base.h:213. Role, judged from paths, function names and nearby code: key wrapping and data encryption at rest. Keys or data encrypted to these public keys are stored: anyone who copies them now decrypts them once a CRQC exists (harvest now, decrypt later).
findings.impact: Long-term risk depends on what the algorithm protects: signatures (authenticity until migration) or key exchange/encryption (retroactive decryption of recorded data).
findings.recommendation: Wrap keys with ML-KEM or a hybrid KEM (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) and re-wrap the stored keys; data that may already have been copied needs its own assessment.
findings.limitations: This is a forward-looking risk that depends on the arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). No such computer is publicly known to exist today; the timeline is uncertain. It is not a present-day exploitable vulnerability. Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — factoring
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks RSA at every key length: a longer modulus only raises the cost polynomially. Plan migration to ML-KEM (or a hybrid) for key establishment and ML-DSA / SLH-DSA for signatures; start with keys protecting data that must stay confidential for years (harvest now, decrypt later) and with long-lived signatures.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Needs a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Published estimates for RSA-2048 fell from 20 million noisy qubits and 8 hours (Gidney–Ekerå 2021) to under a million noisy qubits and under a week (Gidney 2025); a 2026 neutral-atom design puts RSA-2048 one to two orders of magnitude slower than P-256 on 26,000 qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions; no such machine is publicly known.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — discrete logarithms in finite fields
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks finite-field Diffie–Hellman and DSA at every size. Move key establishment to ML-KEM (hybrid with X25519 or ECDH during the transition) and signatures to ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Gidney–Ekerå (2021) estimate RSA and finite-field discrete logarithms together; the resources are of the same order. Ekerå–Gärtner (2024) compare the current algorithm variants for safe-prime and Schnorr groups.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

quantum_algorithms.name: Quantum lattice sieving
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: No change for ML-KEM or ML-DSA at the standard parameter sets. A 2024 claim of a polynomial-time quantum LWE algorithm was withdrawn after a bug was found (see claims).
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Needs exponential memory. The Kyber submission sizes its parameters with core-SVP costs of 2^{0.292β} classical and 2^{0.265β} quantum (e.g. 166 quantum bits for Kyber768).

scenario.rationale: Inside the 10-year horizon the survey puts at 28-49% ('quite possible'), and consistent with the BSI estimate of 15 years that 'could shrink to 10 or even less'. Use it for data that must stay confidential for decades, where being wrong is expensive.
